newsitem.title: RUSSIA: As reform creeps, patience props up Russian army.
newsitem.headline: As reform creeps, patience props up Russian army.

text.p: The sound of shovels echoed under the Moscow ring road as a squad of teenaged army conscripts laboured to shore up a crumbling Soviet-era flyover.

They had not been paid since July. Even when they are, it is just $25 a month. Yet they plodded on, in grubby khaki and clumsy boots, propping up with true Russian patience the slowly collapsing structure of the once mighty Soviet army.
That patience may be about to snap, says Alexander Lebed, the paratrooper drafted in as Kremlin security chief in June.
Lebed, who was flying to Brussels on Sunday for talks with Moscow's old enemy NATO, has warned of mutiny in the ranks if the government does not start paying its debts to the military.

Yet few expect a mass rising by the long-suffering troops -- the army is divided, its men resigned, its officers loyal. But there are fears of crime, theft of weapons and equipment and desertion. Suicide is on the rise.

Lebed's typically outspoken alarm helped elicit a review of current defence spending at the first meeting on Friday of a new Defence Council which made a start on a long-delayed overhaul of Russia's oversized and underfunded armed forces.

"I am taking this issue under special control," said President Boris Yeltsin, who is in hospital preparing for heart surgery. "Russia must have a modern and professional army. Serving in it must be a source of respect and prestige."

Yeltsin promised during this year's re-election campaign to end conscription by 2000 -- a vote-winning move after the carnage among teenagers in Chechnya -- and to create a new-look all-professional army geared to the post-Cold War world.

After five years of delay since it inherited the bulk of the Soviet war machine, Moscow may finally be starting to reform it. The Defence Council officials said there were too many generals and too much red tape. The worst units should go.
Defence Minister Igor Rodionov sacked six top generals on Friday, a move taken as a sign he may finally be overcoming some of the resistance he met after being appointed in July.

But Rodionov, who wants to cut the armed forces to 1.2 million from 1.5 million, is the first to admit it will take time to change the military monolith -- not least because it will cost huge sums to replace conscripts with regulars.

Interfax news agency said on Sunday that the minister would visit the Far East this week to check social conditions and assess the military's readiness for action. The Pacific region has a large military presence and poor conditions.
Newly appointed Defence Council Secetary Yuri Baturin believes Russia needs much longer to professionalise the army than Yeltsin promised.

"I'd like someone to tell me what the Russian economy will look like in two years before making such far-reaching predictions." Baturin said on Saturday. "I rather share the opinion of the defence minister that this can be done by 2005."
So as the Kremlin's Defence Council mulled over the future on Friday, the soldiers on the road gang were left to the more pressing concerns of the present.

"The quicker we finish this bridge, the quicker we'll get paid," said the senior lieutenant, who asked not to be named. His squad has hired itself out to Moscow city council: "At least they pay, unlike the defence ministry," he said.
Like the Soviet-built bridge straining to cope with a surge in traffic that market reform has brought to the capital, Russia's defence structure is not adapted to the 21st century.
The lieutenant said his sappers, once scorned in the Soviet army, were now envied for being able to find work. His father in the elite strategic missile forces had not been paid all year.
Elsewhere in the services, the stories are much the same.
"We're living from hand to mouth," Galina Taranovskaya, a major's wife living in barracks at Volgograd, said last week.
Her husband has not been paid since July and her biggest fear now, with the Russian winter fast approaching, was being unable to afford warm clothes for her two children.
One officer in the barracks shot himself under the strain.
"I don't earn enough even to feed my baby," said Lieutenant Vadim Yegorov, recently transferred to Volgograd from Chechnya. "She's sick but I don't have enough money for medicine."

"The army is only kept on its feet because of the romantic, pure, humane way its officers regard the service," another junior officer said. "As for the future, we don't see any for ourselves. All we can do is survive this terrible time."
